claims.text: The as-deformed CoCrFeMnNi alloy is single-phase.
The untreated as-deformed alloy has high residual stress and a relatively coarse microstructure.
Controlled deformation followed by short-duration annealing can produce a refined or amorphous near-surface layer.
Wear-induced deformation creates a uniform amorphous/nanocrystalline surface layer.
A highly refined, near-amorphous surface film can contribute to low friction and high wear resistance.
The refined amorphous/nanocrystalline layer enhances oxide-film formation.
The refined layer accelerates atomic diffusion.
The refined layer provides abundant nucleation sites for a protective oxide film.
The oxide film rapidly repassivates after mechanical disruption and therefore behaves as a self-healing passive layer.
Rapidly reforming passive oxide simultaneously reduces mechanical wear and corrosion susceptibility.
The self-healing passive film is the governing cause of the coupled tribo-corrosion response.
Samples with the engineered refined surface will have lower wear rates than untreated samples in the corrosive test environment.
Samples with the engineered refined surface will have lower corrosion current densities than untreated samples.
The benefit will occur at moderate sliding speeds and loads where the dynamic oxide layer remains intact.
The benefit will diminish under loading sufficient to remove the oxide completely or in environments that prevent oxide reformation.
The untreated baseline has a coarser, non-uniform microstructure and lacks the tailored refined surface layer.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis describes the refined layer as forming dynamically through wear, whereas the intervention and experimental design treat it as a pre-existing layer produced by deformation and annealing before tribo-corrosion testing. The mechanism does not clearly distinguish formation during pretreatment from further refinement during sliding.
